# Multimodal Models {#sec-multimodal}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Chapter status: drafted.** The measurements use `gemma3:27b` through
`ollama` 0.24.0 on a local GPU, and pages rendered with `Pillow` 12.3.0 from
the WMT16/17/18 tr-en test sets — the same aligned corpus @sec-machine-translation
and @sec-turkish-nlp used, so the Turkish and English pages say the same thing
and a gap between them cannot be a content gap. Scoring used NumPy 2.5.2 on
Python 3.14.5.
:::

**Learning objectives.** After this chapter you can:

- explain how an image becomes tokens, and say what that costs in the units
  you are billed in;
- describe contrastive vision–language pretraining and what it buys
  [@radford2021clip];
- predict where a vision–language model will fail on documents, and why
  resolution is the variable that decides it;
- design the control that separates a model reading an image from a model
  answering plausibly;
- decide whether a VLM or a dedicated OCR pipeline is the right tool for a
  document task.

The scope is document images and vision–language models; audio and video are
outside this chapter. One pointer for speech, because it follows the same
pattern: a speech recogniser such as
[Whisper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.04356) turns audio into a spectrogram (a
picture of which frequencies are loud at each moment, one column every 10 ms)
and feeds it to a transformer encoder; a decoder then writes the transcript.
Audio is processed in 30-second windows, padded if shorter, so the encoder
always produces the same 1,500 vectors per window — the same fixed-budget idea
as the image encoder below.

## An image is a fixed number of tokens {#sec-multimodal-tokens}

A transformer takes a sequence of vectors. @sec-transformers never cared where
those vectors came from, and that is the whole trick: cut an image into
patches, project each patch to the model's hidden size
([**patch embedding**](#gloss-patch-embedding){#term-patch-embedding .term-ref}),
and you have a sequence the same machinery can read [@dosovitskiy2021image].
That paper's model, the **Vision Transformer (ViT)**, is the template for
the vision encoders in this chapter. Each patch also gets a position
embedding, as words do in @sec-transformers, so the model knows *where* on the
image a patch came from.

::: {#gloss-patch-embedding .column-margin .term-gloss}
**Patch embedding** — an image cut into fixed squares, each projected to the
model's hidden size, so a picture becomes a sequence of vectors a transformer
can read alongside text. [↩](#term-patch-embedding){.term-back}
:::

Text tokens and image patches sit in one stream, and attention runs over both.
The usual causal mask still applies: a text token can attend to every image
vector before it, but an image vector cannot look ahead at text that comes
later. (Gemma 3, this chapter's model, additionally lets the vectors of one
image attend to each other in both directions.)

::: {.fig-cap}
There is no separate cross-attention pathway inside the decoder **in this design** — @sec-multimodal-contrastive
describes the alternative, where a frozen language model attends into the image
through cross-attention instead. Patches become vectors, the question
becomes vectors, and one sequence goes into the same stack — which is why a
model that can read text can be taught to read pages without changing its
architecture.
:::
::::

The consequence people skip is what this does to your bill, and it is
measurable in one line. Every image in this chapter's experiment — 320 of
them, four font sizes, two languages, large type and tiny type — cost
**exactly the same 290 prompt tokens**:

```text
  font size  prompt tokens   lines the page can hold at this size
       34 px           290   ~5, comfortable
       22 px           290   ~7
       15 px           290   ~10
       11 px           290   ~14, tight
```

Every page in that ladder carries the *same* sentence; the last column is page
capacity, not content. Holding the content constant is the point of the design,
so the only thing varying is how many encoder pixels each character gets.

Two token counts appear in this chapter, and they measure different things.

- **290** is the *whole prompt* — image plus instruction — as the server
  reports it for the transcription pages.
- **260** is what the image *adds* in the text-versus-image comparison below.
  There the instruction is identical in both arms, so it cancels out.

Wherever this chapter says "as an image, 260", it means this *marginal* cost of
attaching the picture. It matches Gemma 3's published prompt format: 256 image
vectors plus four marker tokens around them (the delimiters — a start-of-image
and an end-of-image token, each with a line break). Do not try to rebuild the
290 from parts: 260 plus the 34-token instruction would come to 294, not 290,
so the two measurements count the delimiters or the instruction differently,
and this run did not keep the raw tokenizer output that would say which. Each
figure is what its own measurement reported.

[For this model, an image costs a flat rate.]{.hl} The vision encoder resizes
every image to 896×896 pixels and cuts it into 14×14-pixel patches: 896 / 14 =
64 patches per side, so 64 × 64 = 4,096 patches. Average pooling over each 4×4
block of patches then shrinks that 64×64 grid to 16×16 = 256 vectors. These are
*soft tokens*: vectors fed straight into the language model rather than looked
up in its vocabulary, but they occupy sequence positions and are billed like
tokens. So 256 image tokens plus the prompt is what you pay whether the page
holds a sentence or a spreadsheet — provided the image is roughly square and
the model's crop-and-tile path does not fire. A wide screenshot split into crops sends each
crop through the encoder separately and costs a multiple of this.

**Do not generalise the flat rate.** It is a property of one encoder design, not
of vision-language models. The dominant 2025–2026 families do the opposite:
dynamic-resolution encoders map a native-resolution image to a *variable*-length
token sequence, and tiling designs cut a page into fixed crops and scale the
number of crops with the input, so image cost grows with megapixels and the
budgeting lesson inverts. Measure your own model with one image at two
resolutions before you plan a bill around either behaviour.

Two things follow, and the second one predicts the rest of the chapter.

**Pixels are an expensive way to send text.** Measured on the same sentences,
sent both ways:

```text
                chars   as text   as image   premium
  English         222      46.6        260     5.57x
  Turkish         233      62.4        260     4.17x
```

If you already have the text, photographing it costs four to five times more
for the same content — a premium paid by every pipeline that screenshots a
page it has already parsed.

Look at the two rows together, though, because they say something less
obvious. The image rate is flat, so **the premium is smaller for Turkish** —
not because pixels are cheaper there, but because @sec-turkish-nlp's tokenizer
penalty makes the *text* expensive: 62.4 tokens against English's 46.6 for the
same sentence, a 1.34× ratio that falls inside the 1.2–1.6× range that chapter
estimates for matched content.

A flat-rate encoder partially absorbs an agglutinative language's token tax.
Hold that thought until @sec-multimodal-ocr, which measures what you give up to
collect it.

**Smaller type means fewer encoder pixels per character.** The page content is
identical at all four rungs — the same sentence, only drawn smaller — so nothing
about the information on the page changes. What changes is *sampling*. The
encoder resizes every page to 896×896 and cuts it into patches, and below some
glyph height a character does not survive that resize with enough pixels to be
told apart from its neighbours. So if transcription accuracy falls with font
size, that is not the model getting confused; it is a sampling limit you can
compute in advance from your canvas size and the encoder's input resolution.
A worked example: a page 1,792 pixels wide is shrunk by a factor of two to fit
896, so 11-pixel type arrives at the encoder about 5.5 pixels tall — less than
half the height of one 14-pixel patch.

The fixed token budget makes it worse in a second and separate way: because the
encoder emits the same 256 vectors per image regardless, you cannot ask it for
more detail within one image. The levers are to crop the page into pieces and
send each piece as its own image (paying 256 vectors for each), or to render or
scan at a larger size — the fix the rest of this chapter keeps returning to.

**What we will look at.** First where the alignment comes from, because a
projected patch means nothing to a language model until something teaches the
two spaces to agree — along the way we meet the kind of encoder whose fixed,
pooled output makes the image cost flat. Then
the chapter's real experiment: the same sentences rendered at four sizes in two
languages, which turns that bottleneck into a threshold and puts the threshold
in a different place for Turkish than for English. Then a control that asks
whether the model is reading the image at all, which returns an answer sharp
enough to settle the practical question the chapter closes on — whether you
want a vision–language model or an OCR engine.

## Where the alignment comes from {#sec-multimodal-contrastive}

Patches give you a sequence. They do not give you a sequence whose vectors mean
anything to a *language* model — a projected patch is just pixels in a new
basis. Something has to teach the two spaces to agree, and the answer that
made everything since possible is contrastive pretraining.

CLIP [@radford2021clip] is the canonical version of
[**contrastive pretraining**](#gloss-contrastive-pretraining){#term-contrastive-pretraining .term-ref}
and the idea is one sentence long: take a large collection of images with their
captions, encode each image and each caption, and train so that **matching pairs
land near each other and mismatched pairs land apart**. Nothing labels what is in
the image. The caption is the supervision, and the internet supplies both halves
for free.

::: {#gloss-contrastive-pretraining .column-margin .term-gloss}
**Contrastive pretraining** — training an image encoder and a text encoder
together so that a picture and its caption land close in one space, and
mismatched pairs land apart. The captions are the supervision, so no one
labels anything. [↩](#term-contrastive-pretraining){.term-back}
:::

::: {.column-margin}
Which is the same bargain @sec-pretraining described for text: the supervision
was already lying around, and the trick was noticing it counted as
supervision. Every scaling story in this book has that shape.
:::

**How "near" and "apart" become a loss.** Take a batch of *N* image–caption
pairs. Encode all of them, normalise the vectors, and compute the cosine
similarity of every image with every caption: an *N* × *N* table whose diagonal
holds the true pairs and whose other *N*² − *N* cells are mismatches. CLIP then
treats each row as a classification problem — "which of these *N* captions
belongs to this image?" — and applies softmax cross-entropy with the diagonal
cell as the right answer; it does the same down each column, for "which image
belongs to this caption?". A learned temperature scales the similarities before
the softmax. This is the InfoNCE loss with in-batch negatives that
@sec-retrieval uses to train dense retrievers, with images in place of
queries. SigLIP [@zhai2023sigmoid], the variant behind this chapter's model,
replaces the softmax with an independent yes/no (sigmoid) decision for every
cell of the table, so no cell needs to be normalised against the whole batch.

Two consequences are worth carrying forward.

**It buys zero-shot classification.** Because captions are text, the label
space is open: to ask *is this a defective weld*, encode one caption per
candidate answer — "a photo of a defective weld", "a photo of a sound weld" —
and pick the one closest to the image. You are no longer restricted to the categories someone enumerated at
training time, which is what made vision models useful in places nobody had
labelled a dataset for.

**It buys a shared space, which is what a VLM is built on.** A shared space is
not the same as intelligibility: nothing about CLIP's geometry makes an
arbitrary language model able to read those vectors. What it gives you is a
visual representation organised by *meaning* rather than by pixels, which is a
good starting point for a learned bridge — and every design below trains that
bridge. With one available, two architectures become possible, and they are
worth separating because they are architecturally opposite and they cost
different things.

*Cross-attention.* Flamingo [@alayrac2022flamingo] **freezes** the language
model entirely, compresses a variable number of patches into a fixed set of
latents with a resampler, and inserts gated cross-attention blocks between the
frozen layers. The image never enters the text sequence at all; it is a second
pathway the text attends *into*. Cheaper to train than updating the whole
model, since the language model's weights never change, and it leaves the
language model's text behaviour untouched.

*Projection into one sequence.* LLaVA [@liu2023visual] does the simpler thing: a
small projector — a single linear layer in the original LLaVA, a two-layer MLP
in its successor LLaVA-1.5 — projects each patch vector to the language model's hidden size, those
vectors are concatenated with the text tokens. Training has two stages: first
only the projector is trained for alignment, then the projector and the language
model are instruction-tuned together, with the vision encoder frozen throughout. One stream, one attention, no new modules — which is the
design in the figure above, and the one most open VLMs now follow.

Knowing which you have in front of you tells you what you can change. Be
precise about what "frozen" rules out: gradients still flow *through* a frozen
language model, which is exactly how the resampler and the gates get trained —
what is frozen is the language model's own weights, so its text-only
behaviour cannot drift. The *system* still learns through the image path: the
resampler and gates are trained, and they change what the frozen model does
whenever an image is present. A single-stream model, by contrast, has no
separate cross-attention pathway inside the decoder to intervene on — its
separate modules are the vision encoder and the projector in front of it.

The vision encoder in this chapter's model is a descendant of CLIP trained with
the sigmoid loss described above [@zhai2023sigmoid], and its fixed pooled output
size is why an image costs a flat rate here.

What contrastive pretraining does *not* buy is any guarantee about detail. The
objective rewards matching an image to its caption, and a caption describes what
a photograph is *about*, not what every region of it contains. That is the root
of the failure this chapter measures next, and it has been documented since
before the current generation of models: caption models assert objects that are
not in the image [@rohrbach2018object].

## Reading a document, measured {#sec-multimodal-ocr}

Documents are where that missing guarantee about detail is easiest to catch,
because the right answer is written on the page. They are also the obvious
industrial use — scanned invoices, forms, contracts, screenshots of dashboards.
So the question worth answering is not *can it read* — it can — but **where it
stops being able to**, and whether that boundary sits in the same place for
every language.

@sec-turkish-nlp's method transfers directly, and this is the reason to use it
here. Take the WMT16/17/18 Turkish–English test sets, which are professional
translations, so the two languages say the same thing. Render each sentence as
a page image in the same font at four sizes, from a comfortable scan down to a
bad phone photo. Any gap between the two languages cannot be a content gap.

**One caveat this design has to answer and does not.** WMT test sets are about
a decade old and public, so the model may well have memorised some of these
sentences — and a memorised sentence can be "transcribed" without being read,
which pushes CER down. The bias is unlikely to be symmetric: the English side of
WMT is probably copied across the web far more often than the Turkish side, so
contamination would inflate exactly the ratio this section reports. The control
is a ladder on sentences published after the model's training cutoff, and it
has not been run. Until it is, treat the roughly 5× gap reported below as an
upper bound.

Two scores. **Character error rate (CER)** — the edit distance between the
model's output and the reference (the smallest number of character
insertions, deletions and substitutions that turns one into the other), divided
by the reference length — for overall damage. And **diacritic retention** — of
the `ç ğ ı ö ş ü İ` that should be on the page, how many survived — because a
model that quietly strips Turkish diacritics (the reverse of the
deasciification @sec-turkish-nlp describes) is doing something specific, and
CER alone would hide it inside a general error rate.

```text
gemma3:27b, 40 aligned sentence pairs, one font, four sizes

 language   font px    CER    diacritics kept  prompt tokens
  English       34   0.04%                  —            290
  English       22   0.05%                  —            290
  English       15   0.22%                  —            290
  English       11   1.33%                  —            290
  Turkish       34   0.26%              99.8%            290
  Turkish       22   0.25%              99.6%            290
  Turkish       15   1.30%              99.3%            290
  Turkish       11   6.67%              95.1%            290
```

### What it says

[Turkish costs about five times the error rate of English on identical content,
measured firmly at 11 px and consistent with every rung above it.]{.hl} 6.5× at 34 px, 5.0× at 22, 5.9× at 15, 5.0× at 11.

Before reading that as four confirmations, convert the percentages back into
events. Forty sentences is about 8,880 English characters and 9,320 Turkish
ones, so the top two English rungs are **about four wrong characters each**
(3.6 and 4.4 on average), and the Turkish ones are about twenty-four and
twenty-three. A ratio of two counts that
small carries an enormous interval — the 6.5× at 34 px is 24 edits against 3.6 —
so "remarkably stable" is the wrong description. The rung that is statistically
solid is the bottom one, where the counts are 622 against 118, and the honest
reading is **one ratio measured firmly at 11 px and not contradicted anywhere
above it**. What changes down the ladder is the absolute damage, and at 11
pixels it becomes a real number — 6.67% of characters wrong against English's
1.33%.

This is @sec-turkish-nlp's pattern arriving through a door that chapter never
opened. On the *input* side there is no tokenizer, no stemmer, no lowercasing —
just pixels and a vision encoder. And the tool still works measurably worse in
Turkish, still without raising anything you could catch in a log. The output
side is a different matter: the transcript is still written token by token by
the same language model, through the same tokenizer, and the next subsection
shows that its errors look like the language model's guesses. So the gap is not
"vision without language"; it is a vision input feeding a language model that
may itself be weaker in Turkish, and this experiment cannot say how much of the
gap comes from each side.

Note also **where the cliff is**. Between 22 px and 15 px, English degrades by
a factor of four from a tiny number; Turkish degrades by a factor of five to a
number you would notice. Between 15 px and 11 px, both degrade again — English
by a factor of six, Turkish by five.

So the two curves have the same shape; Turkish is the English curve shifted up
by a roughly constant factor. What that shift does in practice is move the
*threshold*. Pick any error rate you can tolerate — say 1% of characters —
and Turkish crosses it at a larger font size than English (between 22 and
15 px here, against between 15 and 11 px for English). The degradation accelerates
at each step, so for a fixed tolerance resolution behaves not like a smooth
dial but like a threshold, and for a fixed tolerance the threshold sits at
a different place for the two languages — which means a scanning setting
validated on English documents is not validated for Turkish ones.

### The failure is not the one you would predict

I expected the errors to be diacritics: `ş` read as `s`, `ğ` as `g`. Some of
that happens — diacritic retention falls to 95.1% at 11 px, so roughly one in
twenty Turkish-specific characters vanishes. But it is a minority of the
damage, and the majority is more interesting.

```text
REF  ... ailesinin Mississippi, Greenville banliyölerinde bulunan evine ...
HYP  ... ailesinin Mississippi, Greenville'de bulunan evine ...
```

The model did not drop a diacritic or garble a letter. It replaced a word it
could not resolve with a **shorter, grammatical, plausible** alternative. That
is not OCR failing; that is a language model doing what language models do —
filling an uncertain region with something likely — and it is the specific
reason a VLM is a different risk profile from a classical OCR engine.

A dedicated OCR system, when it fails on a character it cannot resolve, tends
to produce something visibly wrong. A VLM produces *fluent Turkish that was
never on the page*. Treat that as a difference of degree rather than a clean
rule: modern OCR engines also use language models and lexicons, and they will
happily turn one plausible digit or word into another plausible one. What
changes with a VLM is how much of the output can be reconstructed from priors
and how little of it announces itself as a guess.

::: {.column-margin}
Which gives a practical rule you can enforce: if a downstream step will treat the
transcription as ground truth, prefer a tool whose failures look like
failures. @sec-multimodal-tools names the dedicated OCR engines. Use the VLM
where the task is understanding rather than transcription — *what is this
document about*, *which field is the total* — and where a wrong answer is
checked by something other than its own fluency.
:::

## Does it read the image, or answer plausibly? {#sec-multimodal-hallucination}

The transcription result raises a sharper question. If the model fills
illegible regions with likely text, how much of *any* answer it gives about an
image is actually coming from the pixels?

That is answerable with the control this book keeps returning to. Render
tables of **invented** figures — Turkish city names against numbers no model
could know or guess — and ask two kinds of question about each:

- **present**: a row that is in the table. Scored on exact match.
- **absent**: a plausible Turkish city that is *not* in the table. Scored on
  whether the model says so.

The second is the whole experiment. A model that answers everything
confidently is indistinguishable from a model that reads well, right up until
you ask it something the image does not contain.

```text
gemma3:27b, 30 tables of 8 invented rows, 180 questions

  value present in the table   read correctly   89/90  =  98.9%
  value NOT in the table       refused          90/90  = 100.0%
```

**It refused every single time.** Ninety opportunities to invent a plausible
number for a plausible city, and it took none of them. The one error in the
other column was a misread digit, not an invention.

**The control this contrast needs, and does not have.** These tables were
rendered at a size the model can comfortably read; the transcription failure it
is being contrasted with happens at 11 pixels, where the page is barely legible.
So the two halves of the chapter's headline are measured in two different
resolution regimes, and the honest question is whether refusal *survives*
illegibility. Re-render the same 30 tables at 11 px and ask the same 180
questions: if the refusal rate holds, the asymmetry is about the kind of
question; if it collapses, the asymmetry was about easy images against hard
ones and the claim inverts. That run is one afternoon and it is the first thing
we would add.

Two more things this section owes you, both of which change how the 100% reads.
A refusal rate is a property of the *prompt* at least as much as of the model —
"write the value, or say it is not in the table" invites refusal in a way that
"what is the value for Trabzon?" does not — and the prompts are not reproduced
here. Nor are the decoding settings: the whole argument is about what
distribution the model emits, so whether this was greedy or sampled is not a
detail. Record both when you run it.

### The two results together are the finding

Read on its own, that table says the model is trustworthy about images. Read
next to @sec-multimodal-ocr, it says something much more specific and much more
useful:

```text
  asked for something that is NOT in the image     refuses, 100%
  asked to transcribe something it CANNOT resolve  invents fluent Turkish
```

[In this test the model refused every absent value. It did not know what it could not read.]{.hl}

The distinction is not a quirk; it follows from how the two questions are
posed. *Is Trabzon in this table* is a categorical judgement the model can make
from evidence that is actually present — it can see the eight rows, and Trabzon
is not among them. *What does this smudge say* has no such evidence to check
against: the region is uncertain, the model's job at every step is to emit a
likely continuation, and a likely continuation is exactly what it emits.

There is no reliable internal signal that separates "I read this" from "I
inferred this", because both come out of the same forward pass. Each output
token does have a probability, but a guess the language model finds likely can
score just as high as a clearly printed word, so a high probability does not
mean the pixels supported the token.

::: {.column-margin}
Compare @sec-decoding's logprob result: token probabilities ranked answers well
but were badly calibrated, and they were most useful for abstaining on a
discrete question. Abstention works when there is a question to abstain on. It
has nothing to act on inside a long generated string, where no single token
announces itself as a guess.
:::

Set the two questions side by side and the asymmetry is in the evidence, not in
the model:

:::: {.anlp-fig}

The left question can be settled against something the model can see; the right
one cannot. It is not more honest on the left — it simply has evidence there
and only a probability distribution on the right, and both answers come out
through the same generation step.
:::
::::

That gives a rule you can hold on to. **Ask a VLM questions.** Do not ask it to
be an OCR engine and then trust the output as a transcript, because its failure
mode is fluent. Do not assume the alternative fails loudly either: a dedicated
engine gives you confidence scores to gate on, which helps, and it can
still turn one plausible word or digit into another. Whichever tool produces
the transcript, validate the fields downstream systems will treat as facts.

## VLM or OCR? {#sec-multimodal-choosing}

That rule is really a claim about tools rather than about models. The two are
not competing implementations of one thing; they have different failure modes,
and the failure mode should pick the tool.

A [**vision-language model (VLM)**](#gloss-vision-language-model-vlm){#term-vision-language-model-vlm .term-ref}
and an [**optical character recognition (OCR)**](#gloss-optical-character-recognition-ocr){#term-optical-character-recognition-ocr .term-ref}
engine are built for different jobs, and it shows in what they do when they are
wrong.

::: {#gloss-vision-language-model-vlm .column-margin .term-gloss}
**Vision-language model (VLM)** — a language model with a vision encoder
attached, so images and text occupy one sequence. Reads pages, charts and
photographs, and answers questions about them.
[↩](#term-vision-language-model-vlm){.term-back}
:::

::: {#gloss-optical-character-recognition-ocr .column-margin .term-gloss}
**Optical character recognition (OCR)** — turning an image of text into text.
A dedicated engine exposes confidence scores (per character, word or line,
depending on the engine) that you can gate on, which is
its main advantage over a model with no such signal; both can make plausible
errors.
[↩](#term-optical-character-recognition-ocr){.term-back}
:::

| | Dedicated OCR | Vision–language model |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Output when confident | text, with confidence scores per word or line (per character in some engines) | text; token probabilities exist but do not say whether the pixels supported the token |
| Output when it fails | [often visibly wrong, with confidences to gate on — plausible substitutions happen too]{.pro} | [fluent, plausible, wrong]{.con} |
| Layout and reading order | needs its own model or heuristics | [handled, often well]{.pro} |
| Answering *about* a document | [not its job — you build that on top]{.con} | [the thing it is for]{.pro} |
| Charts and diagrams | [nothing useful]{.con} | reads them, with the caveat above |
| Cost per page | cheap, local; classical engines (Tesseract) run comfortably on CPU, deep-learning engines benefit from a GPU | for this model's fixed-grid encoder, a flat 256+ tokens plus generation; tiling encoders charge per crop |
| Turkish specifically | depends entirely on the engine's language packs | measured above: ~5× the English error rate at 11 px |

: Two tools, two failure modes {tbl-colwidths="[24,36,40]"}

The practical architecture for document work in 2026 is usually **both**: a
dedicated engine produces the transcript, and the VLM answers questions over
the transcript *and* the image. That way the text you index comes with
confidences you can gate on, and the model is used for the part it is uniquely good at
— reading layout, finding the field, understanding the chart.

## Intuition checks {#sec-multimodal-intuition}

Answer each one before you open it. All six are questions this chapter settled
with a measurement rather than an argument.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. Is sending an image cheaper than sending the text?

No, and it is not close. The same sentence measured both ways cost **46.6
tokens as English text and 260 as an image** — a 5.57× premium, 4.17× in
Turkish. For this encoder the image rate is *flat*, which is the part that surprises people: the
encoder always emits 256 vectors, so a page holding one line and a page holding
fourteen cost the same — and every one of this chapter's 320 pages, from 34-px
to 11-px type, cost exactly 290 prompt tokens. So
photographing text you already have is pure waste, and the waste is larger the
less the page contains.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. Why does transcription accuracy fall as the font gets smaller, if the model is unchanged?

Because the encoder's input resolution and token budget are fixed, so as the
type shrinks each character gets fewer pixels. Be exact about what is being
held constant: the *content* is the same sentence in every row, so nothing new
is being added — what changes is that the characters occupy fewer pixels, and
the encoder emits a fixed number of vectors regardless. A smaller font means
fewer encoder pixels per character through the same bottleneck. You can predict the direction of
this effect before running anything — and it means the fix is resolution and
cropping, not prompting.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. Your VLM reads English documents at 0.2% character error. What will it do on Turkish?

Worse, and by a factor you should measure rather than assume. Here it was
**about 5×, measured firmly at the smallest size** on semantically matched
English and Turkish text rendered under identical conditions — 6.67% against
1.33%; the upper rungs agree but rest on too few errors to count as evidence on
their own. Note that "identical content" is as far as the control goes: both are
Latin script, and the Turkish differs in its diacritics, its word forms and its
morphology as well as its letters, so the experiment isolates the *language*,
not one property of it. The general lesson is @sec-turkish-nlp's, arriving with no
tokenizer on the input side: a pipeline validated on English is not validated
for another language, even when its input is pixels rather than text.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 4. A VLM transcribed a page and the output reads perfectly. Is it correct?

Not necessarily: fluency is not evidence of transcription accuracy. The
measured failure mode is not garbled characters; it is a word the model could
not resolve replaced by a shorter, grammatical, plausible one — output that
looks better than an honest failure would. A classical engine at least attaches
confidences to what it emits, but it can make plausible substitutions too. If a
downstream step will treat the transcript as truth, compare the two tools'
error rates on your own documents and validate the fields that matter.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 5. Do VLMs hallucinate answers about images?

Less than their reputation, in the case that is easy to test: asked 90 times
for a value that was not in the table, this model refused **90 times**. What it
does do is invent inside things it *is* generating, like a transcript of an
illegible region. Absence it can detect; illegibility it cannot, because
nothing in a forward pass reliably separates reading from inferring.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 6. Should you replace your OCR pipeline with a VLM?

Usually you should run both. Use the dedicated engine for the transcript, so
failures are loud and gateable, and the VLM for the things it is uniquely good
at — layout, locating a field, reading a chart, answering questions about the
page. Replacing a gateable failure mode with a silent one is a downgrade even when
the average accuracy improves.
:::

## Interview questions {#sec-multimodal-interview}

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**On sourcing — the same caveat as @sec-text-as-data.** These recur in the two
credible open sources this book uses, plus the ones this chapter's own
measurements make answerable.
:::

### Testing whether you understand the mechanism

**Q: How does an image get into a language model?**

Cut into patches, each patch projected to the model's hidden size by a vision
encoder, and the resulting vectors concatenated with the text tokens into one
sequence. Attention then runs over that sequence as usual, with the causal
mask letting text attend to the image vectors before it. The consequence worth
adding, because it shows you have used one: this encoder emits a *fixed* number
of vectors, so image cost does not scale with what is on the page — measured
here at a flat 290 prompt tokens for every page from 34-px to 11-px type, of
which the image itself accounts for 260. Then add that tiling and
dynamic-resolution encoders do scale with the image.

**Q: A model reads your documents well in testing and badly in production.
Where do you look?**

Resolution first, because it is the variable with a cliff rather than a slope.
At smaller type the same content gets fewer encoder pixels per character, and
the degradation accelerates at each step, behaving like a threshold for any
fixed tolerance —
here English went from 0.04% to 1.33% character error across the ladder and
Turkish from 0.26% to 6.67%. Then check whether production pages differ from
test pages in language, because the cliff sits in a different place for
different languages and glyph distributions.

### Testing whether you have shipped one

**Q: How would you evaluate a VLM on document extraction?**

With two controls, and say why each exists. First, character error rate against
typed references, broken out by any resolution and language you actually
encounter — the aggregate hides the cliff. Second, an **absence control**:
questions whose answers are not on the page, scored on refusal. Without the
second you cannot distinguish a model that reads from a model that answers
plausibly. And read the worst-case transcripts by hand for passages that are
grammatical and wrong, because that class of error survives every automatic
check you are likely to run.

**Q: When would you not use a VLM?**

When you need a transcript that a downstream system will trust. The failure
mode is fluent and hard to detect from the output itself, so a silent error
propagates into whatever you index or compute. Use a dedicated OCR engine there, keep the VLM for
understanding rather than transcription, and if you need both, run both — the
extra cost is small next to a wrong number nobody caught.

## Lab: find your own resolution cliff {#sec-multimodal-lab}

The number you are after is the resolution below which your own documents stop
being readable — and it is specific to your pages, your fonts and your
language, so nobody can give it to you.

### Step 1 — twenty real pages, not clean ones

Take twenty documents from your actual pipeline, including the bad scans.
Clean test data is the reason resolution problems reach production.

### Step 2 — build the ladder

Render or downsample each page at four resolutions spanning comfortable to
marginal. You are looking for a threshold, so you need points either side of it.

### Step 3 — transcribe and score with edit distance

You need reference text for twenty pages. Type it. It is two hours and it is
the only part of this lab that cannot be skipped, because every number
afterwards depends on it.

### Step 4 — score the language-specific characters separately

Count how many of your language's diacritics survived. A general error rate
averages this away, and it is the part that breaks downstream matching.

### Step 5 — run the absence control

Ask ten questions whose answers are *not* on the page. Count confident
answers. Do the same for ten that are.

### Step 6 — find where the fluent inventions start

Read the transcriptions at your worst resolution by hand and mark every
passage that is grammatical and wrong. That count, not the character error
rate, is what tells you whether the output is safe to index.

### What to hand in

The error-rate ladder with the cliff marked, the diacritic retention at each
step, the two control counts, and one sentence naming the minimum resolution
you would accept in production.

## Exercises {#sec-multimodal-exercises}

1. **Predict, then check.** Collect three images from your own work — a table
   scan, a chart, a photo. Predict which one the model will misread and how,
   *in writing*, before testing. Then check. The value of this exercise is
   entirely in having written the prediction down.
2. **Find your cliff.** Take one page and render it at eight resolutions.
   Plot character error rate against resolution. Is it a slope or a step? Mark
   the resolution you would set as a minimum, and say what it costs to
   guarantee it.
3. **The absence control.** Write ten questions whose answers are not in a
   document you have. Ask them. Count confident answers. If the count is zero,
   make the questions harder — plausible-sounding fields that a similar
   document *would* have — and try again.
4. **Fluent and wrong.** Transcribe five pages at your worst realistic
   resolution and mark every passage that is grammatical and not on the page.
   Compare that count to the character error rate. Which one would have
   warned you?
5. **Two languages, one content.** If you work in more than one language, find
   or make an aligned pair and run the ladder on both. Report the ratio. If it
   is near 1, you have evidence your pipeline generalises; if it is 5, you have
   a number to take to whoever sets the scanning policy.
6. **Price it.** Compute what your document volume costs as images versus as
   text, using the flat image rate you measure for your own model. Then find
   the place in your pipeline that sends an image of text it already had.
7. **The hybrid.** Build the two-tool architecture from
   @sec-multimodal-choosing on ten documents: dedicated OCR for the transcript,
   VLM for the questions. Measure whether the combination beats either alone on
   your task, and say what it costs.

## What to remember {#sec-multimodal-summary}

- **An image is a flat rate — for this encoder.** Every one of the 320 pages in
  this chapter cost the same **290 prompt tokens** — 256 image vectors, a few
  marker tokens and the prompt — regardless of font size or content, because this model resizes to a
  fixed grid and pools to a fixed 256 vectors. Dynamic-resolution and tiling
  encoders, which most 2025–2026 families use, charge a variable number instead.
  Look up your own encoder's rule before budgeting; that it *has* one is the
  useful part.
- **Photographing text you already have costs about 4.2–5.6×.** The same sentence: 46.6
  tokens as English text, 62.4 as Turkish text, **260 as an image**. The
  premium is *smaller* for Turkish only because @sec-turkish-nlp's tokenizer
  penalty already made the text expensive.
- **Resolution is a cliff, not a slope, and the cliff is language-specific.**
  At smaller type the same content occupies fewer pixels per character; the
  experiment changes readability, not the amount of source information. English went 0.04% → **1.33%** character error
  across the ladder; Turkish went 0.26% → **6.67%**.
- **Turkish cost about 5× the error rate of English at 11 px** (a firm
  measurement; the upper rungs agree but are not evidence on their own), on
  professionally translated pairs where the content was identical. No
  tokenizer, stemmer or `lower()` on the input side — just pixels, and the tool
  still worked measurably worse in Turkish. @sec-turkish-nlp's pattern
  does not need a text *input* to appear; the output is still written by a
  language model.
- **The failure mode is fluency, not garbage.** Diacritic loss was the minority
  of the damage (95.1% retained at the worst setting). The majority was a word
  the model could not resolve, replaced with a shorter, grammatical, plausible
  one. A VLM fails in correct Turkish; do not assume a classical engine cannot.
- **In this test the model refused every absent value; it did not know what it
  could not read.** Asked 90 times for a value absent from a table, it refused
  **90 times** — zero misses, which under independence still allows a miss rate
  up to about 3.3%, and 90 questions drawn from 30 tables are not fully
  independent — and
  read the present values at 98.9%. Absence is checkable against evidence;
  illegibility is not, because nothing in a forward pass reliably separates
  reading from inferring.
- **So use both tools.** Dedicated OCR for the transcript, where failures come
  with confidences you can gate on; the VLM for layout, locating fields, charts, and questions
  about the page. Replacing a gateable failure mode with a silent one is a
  downgrade even when average accuracy improves.
